newsitem.title: USA: Satellites take distance out of learning.
newsitem.headline: Satellites take distance out of learning.

text.p: Distance learning, once carried out exclusively through the mail, has long been viewed as the poor relation of physically attending classes.
With the advent of satellites all that has now changed, allowing students to attend lectures from thousands of miles away and even ask questions via telephone as if they were actually on campus.
The California State University this week launched a distance learning programme that uses satellites to create a virtual classroom, offering students access to the university from remote areas.

Classes from seven of California State's campuses are beamed to a Hughes Communications satellite 22,300 miles above the Earth's surface and then sent to 31 other Cal State locations throughout the state.

Students as far north as Crescent City and as far south as Imperial Valley, almost a thousand miles apart, get the same classroom experience without having to relocate to another city or commute large distances.
The Internet has also enabled long-distance students to interact more readily with professors.

Molly Corbett Broad, executive vice-chancellor at the university, said the need to enhance distance learning programmes grew from the realisation that state funding was not going to cover the costs of building the extra classrooms needed to accommodate increasing student demand.
"We don't have enough physical facilities ... to cope with the anticipated increases, but with distance learning we can still expand access to the university," Broad said.

Adri Jimerfield, a 60-year old divorced woman with four grown children, is in her second semester. She takes classes with six other women in Grass Valley, a small rural town about two hours away from the nearest campus at Chico.
These lectures are beamed to the community college in Grass Valley from Chico.
Jimerfield, who works as a careers and life counsellor at Bear River High School, could not study for her degree in sociology and career planning if she had to commute to Chico.
"It would be very difficult (to commute) because I work a full-time very demanding job," Jimerfield said.

"I went to community college for the first part of my education and then I transferred and I thought I would miss the interaction of a classroom, but I'm in a room with six or seven women and ... it's very stimulating," she said.
"Once a semester we car pool and visit one of our professors and get acquainted. It's been wonderful, it's a surprise," she said.
The satellite programme now offers 350 classes, allowing students to obtain bachelor and master degrees in courses as diverse as social science and criminology.
Jimmerfield hopes the satellite learning programme will help her achieve her long standing goal of running her own business.
"My goal, when I retire in five years at 65, is to have a private practice counselling people for careers," she said.
